youtube.title: The exit | Meanwhile, Inside No. 006
youtube.caption:
How does this cell leave your blood? This wall has no open door.

Where tissue is inflamed, the wall turns sticky, and the cell rolls. Then its grips switch on, and it stops. It crawls to a seam between two wall cells. In a rare inherited condition, those grips are faulty. Cells roll on past. So pus is mostly white cells from your blood. Each one let itself out.

Series: Season 1: The traffic inside you, part 6 of 6. Next: The spark

Sources
1. A venule's lining has no ready-made opening for a white cell: neighbouring wall cells meet at closed, regulated junctions, and the leukocyte generates its own micron-scale gap (or a pore through one wall cell) as it squeezes through; this did not need the wall cells to contract (the older view was that the wall cells contract to let it through). — doaj.org: https://doaj.org/article/10960c2cd30d4e339fbdac6278b6f396
2. In adults, neutrophils are the most numerous circulating white blood cell: about 60-70% of a normal white count of about 4,000-11,000 cells per microlitre. — NCBI (NIH): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK570571/
3. A neutrophil suspended in fluid (round, roughly as in blood) measures about 8.3-8.4 µm across (range about 7.3-9.7 µm), the largest leukocyte type in that study. — bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu: https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=100510
4. At a site of tissue damage (inflammation), white blood cells move out of the circulation and collect in the damaged tissue, outside the vessels; in a pus-forming lesion those cells are mostly neutrophils. — Britannica: https://britannica.com/story/how-is-inflammation-involved-in-swelling
5. Virchow and some of his followers held that pus cells arose inside the inflamed tissue's own connective-tissue cells ('connective tissue corpuscles'), not from the blood; in the 1860s this was the accepted theory that Cohnheim's work undermined. — NCBI (NIH): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9775877/
6. Cohnheim's first article on inflammation and pus, 'Ueber Entzündung und Eiterung', which reported his frog experiments, appeared in Virchow's Archiv in 1867 (vol. 40, pp. 1-79). — historyofmedicine.com: https://historyofmedicine.com/id/2941
7. Cohnheim worked under Virchow at the Pathological Institute in Berlin (Britannica: 1865-68; Wikipedia and the Jewish Encyclopedia: assistant from autumn 1864 to 1868), so in 1867 he was Virchow's assistant. — Britannica: https://www.britannica.com:443/print/article/124621
8. Cohnheim exposed the mesentery of a living frog paralysed with curare ('woorara') and watched its vessels under the microscope. — NCBI (NIH): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9799538/
9. Inflammatory signals (such as IL-1 and TNF) make the vessel lining express E-selectin, which is largely inactive on resting endothelium; P-selectin on the endothelium is needed for leukocyte rolling in mice. These lining molecules are what make an inflamed vessel's wall 'sticky' for passing white cells. — frontiersin.org: https://frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1401399/full
10. Selectins on the endothelium (the vessel's lining) tether passing leukocytes and make them roll. — NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4592324
11. After arrest, neutrophils crawl along the inside of the vessel to distant emigration sites, using the integrin Mac-1 gripping ICAM-1; cells that cannot crawl start to transmigrate close to where they stopped and are slower to get out. — rupress.org: https://rupress.org/jem/article/203/12/2569/46312/Intraluminal-crawling-of-neutrophils-to-emigration
12. Most neutrophils leave between two endothelial cells (paracellular); in mouse venules 60-85 µm wide, fewer than 15% went through a single wall cell (transcellular). — NCBI (NIH): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11196655/
13. In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, a rare inherited condition (incidence estimated at about 1 in a million), mutations in the gene for CD18, the shared subunit of the beta-2 integrins, leave those grips missing, too few or not working, so leukocytes cannot migrate out to infection sites; blood white counts are typically high and pus often fails to form. — statpearls.com: https://www.statpearls.com/point-of-care/24214
14. Neutrophils from a patient with CD18 deficiency (LAD-I) rolled normally along living venules but could not stick or emigrate when stimulated: they roll on instead of stopping. — jci.org: https://www.jci.org/articles/view/116535
15. Squeezing leukocyte nuclei open gaps about 4-5 µm wide in the vessel lining, about half to three-fifths of the round neutrophil's 8.3 µm (c3). — weizmann.ac.il: https://www.weizmann.ac.il/dept/irb/Alon/node/343
…and 5 more in the pinned comment.

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. Every number is checked against the sources.

Meanwhile, Inside: What your body is doing right now, while you watch.

When a neutrophil crosses between two wall cells, a gap opens in the VE-cadherin junction as it passes and closes again once it is through: in time-lapse imaging of cultured human vessel-lining cells under flow, the gap was closed after full transmigration (by about 265 s in one example), and in another study the crossing took under 5 minutes, with the gap resealing shortly after. — NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2726622
17. Pus is mainly neutrophils, living and dead, with liquefied tissue debris, microbes and fluid; an abscess is a localized collection of it. — medicine.osu.edu: https://medicine.osu.edu/-/media/files/medicine/departments/otolaryngology/atlas-of-head-and-neck-pathology/a/abscess-and-phlegmon.pdf
18. A white cell triggers its own way out: in mice, leukocytes set off the dephosphorylation of VE-cadherin Tyr731 through the phosphatase SHP-2, which lets AP-2 bind and starts VE-cadherin's endocytosis, opening the junction; and leukocytes generate the gaps themselves, without needing the wall cells to contract. — Nature: https://www.nature.com/articles/ni.2824
19. The bone marrow makes neutrophils continuously, at a basal rate of about 5 x 10^10 to 10 x 10^10 a day. — NCBI (NIH): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2930213/
20. Even at a low estimate of 1.5 x 10^10 new neutrophils a day (below every estimate here, including those that use the newer, longer blood half-life of about 19 h), the marrow makes about 174,000 a second: more than ten million by 57.6 s into the film, and about 10.7-11.6 million while the line is spoken. — NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929930
